overview: The atlas label Mordvinians is not a recovered name for one medieval country. It is an external umbrella applied to distinct Erzya and Moksha peoples, whose related languages have separate standards; some people use layered umbrella identities. The imported summary wrongly ties an older Russian exonym to 1928, the year a Soviet administrative district was created. It cannot explain an 800 to 900 layer. That layer is troublesome: its polygon stretches toward the southern Urals, while Saransk and tested Mordovian centers lie outside. Preserve the shape as atlas evidence, not a surveyed ethnic frontier. Archaeology offers graves, ornaments, clothing traces, tools, weapons, horse gear, and changing contacts. It rarely identifies a person's language, family rules, lessons, remedy, or toilet. Later chronicles use an outside collective name; historical linguists propose widely different divergence dates. The eight periods are reading windows, not reigns. A securely sourced 1994 Moksha sentence appears with 2022 grammatical analysis; it illustrates living language, not ninth-century speech. At 900 the map label ends, while communities continue.

periods.title: 800 to 812: a map label arrives without a state
periods.summary: The exact id appears only in the 800 snapshot. Its polygon excludes all tested points in modern Mordovia and reaches Samara, Buzuluk, and Orenburg. Archaeology cannot turn that mismatch into one border. Read the layer as inherited artwork beside independently dated evidence, not as a founding event or government.

periods.title: 812 to 825: cemeteries preserve selected lives
periods.summary: Middle Tsna cemeteries broadly dated from the eighth through eleventh centuries contain both cremations and inhumations, varied orientations, pits, coffins, and grave furnishings. That diversity crosses this narrow reading window. Burials were deliberate selections, so they illuminate mortuary practice without providing a household census or complete social order.

periods.title: 825 to 837: objects travel farther than labels
periods.summary: Ornaments, belt parts, tools, weapons, and horse equipment connect communities to wider Volga and forest-zone networks. Similar forms can move through exchange, travel, copying, marriage, or migration. A shared object does not automatically carry one language or political loyalty, and later Bulgar parallels must not be pulled backward.

periods.title: 837 to 850: language change is reconstructed, not witnessed
periods.summary: Published estimates for divergence leading toward Erzya and Moksha range roughly from the sixth to thirteenth centuries; one reconstruction places late Proto-Mordvin near 1000. No local sentence survives from this window. Linguistic models cannot assign every grave, settlement, or atlas point to one named language.

periods.title: 850 to 862: work leaves uneven traces
periods.summary: Earlier regional archaeology and later medieval collections document farming, animal keeping, fishing, hunting, beekeeping, pottery, metalwork, spinning, and woodworking. Exact ninth-century evidence varies by site. These comparisons suggest possible skill traditions, but the card does not turn a later museum object or an earlier study into a universal 850 CE routine.

periods.title: 862 to 875: neighboring communities remain neighbors
periods.summary: The polygon shares atlas arcs with Khazar, Slavonic, Volga Bulgar, and Bashkir labels, yet the audit finds no area overlap for the exact shape. Shared drawing edges are software geometry, not treaties. Neighboring Muroma archaeology is useful comparison only; Muroma graves cannot be relabeled Erzya, Moksha, or Mordvinian.

periods.title: 875 to 887: learning happened without preserved schools
periods.summary: Making a pot, fastening clothing, handling animals, working metal, navigating rivers, and conducting a burial all required learned sequences. Children participated in communities, but exact ages, teachers, chores, and lesson settings are undocumented. Evidence supports knowledge transfer more securely than a reconstructed classroom, curriculum, or childhood timetable.

periods.title: 887 to 900: the software endpoint is not disappearance
periods.summary: At 900 the exact feature vanishes, while later chronicles, archaeology, languages, and communities continue. The endpoint neither records conquest nor proves that everyone changed identity together. It closes one atlas interval. Later evidence must keep its own date, author, and naming perspective instead of being squeezed into this final thirteen-year window.

items.text: The exact indexed record is mordvinians, dated approximately 800 to 900 and lacking an imported kind. Coverage calls it a state, but supplies no government, ruler, capital, law, or administration. The researched correction is culture, an umbrella teaching card whose map lifetime remains unchanged.

Mordva or Mordvin is an exoethnonym, while Erzya and Moksha are distinct self-identifications and languages. People may also use layered identities, so the card does not dictate a single preferred answer. Its title preserves the searchable atlas label and immediately explains whose names it can blur.

The sole target shape is one polygon with 101 positions and a bounding box from about 45.64 to 56.61 east and 50.91 to 55.31 north. Saransk and four other Mordovian-center probes lie outside; Samara, Tolyatti, Syzran, Buzuluk, and Orenburg lie inside.

The imported summary says an official term grouped Erzya and Moksha from 1928. In fact, the exonym is centuries older; 1928 marks a Soviet administrative district. The replacement separates modern administration, self-identification, historical linguistics, archaeology, and atlas artwork instead of treating them as one fact.

No reviewed evidence shows a centralized Mordvinian state occupying this painted area. Grave groups, material similarities, contacts, and later collective names answer different questions. The card therefore uses communities, makers, and people buried at named sites, never a fictional border patrol checking passports along an atlas arc.

Middle Tsna cemeteries occupy capes and sandy hills near Morshansk. Researchers report cremation and inhumation, multiple grave-pit and coffin forms, and varied body orientations. These patterns demonstrate choices within a broad eighth- to eleventh-century span, not one identical ritual performed everywhere between 800 and 900.

Shoksha's fifth- to eleventh-century graves receive competing Ryazan-Oka, ancient Mordvin, and Muroma-Mordvin classifications. Eighth- to ninth-century Armiyevo also shows local Finnic and Turkic-associated interaction and differs from some synchronous “Mordva” cemeteries. These disputes reveal heterogeneous evidence, not tidy ethnic blocks.

Grave furnishings include ornaments, clothing and headdress traces, tools, weapons, and horse harness. Placement was part of a funeral, so it may express memory, role, relationship, or ritual rather than the deceased person's complete everyday kit. A grave inventory is curated evidence, not a packed suitcase.

Richly furnished and paired burials can suggest social difference and relationships, yet wealth, rank, gender, occupation, and kinship do not follow automatically from object counts. Preservation and excavation also vary. The safest conclusion is that mourners differentiated burials, while the meaning of each difference requires contextual study.

Cemeteries are often easier to recognize than settlements because metal ornaments attract attention and graves form visible clusters. Archaeologists have warned that missing cemeteries can reflect other rites or poor survival. Empty places on a distribution map therefore cannot be treated as uninhabited or culturally uniform.

sections.title: Homes, food, work, and seasonal life

items.text: The exact-period sources reviewed here describe burials more fully than houses. Earlier regional studies and later medieval exhibits document farming, stock keeping, hunting, fishing, beekeeping, pottery, woodworking, textiles, and metalwork. They offer bounded comparisons, not permission to furnish every ninth-century home with one standardized toolkit.

Forest, river, meadow, and cultivated landscapes offered different foods and materials. Later ethnography records grain farming, livestock, bees, fishing, hunting, mushrooms, berries, and nuts, but those details span much later periods. For 800 to 900, the card names broad possibilities only when archaeology or dated comparison supports them.

Pottery could cook and store food; knives, axes, spindle equipment, and metal ornaments show skilled making in later medieval collections. Exact functions depend on context and wear. A small clay object might be a weight, toy, or something else, so cheerful guesses never outrank an excavator's evidence.

Horse harness in some graves shows that horses mattered in selected mortuary displays and perhaps travel or status. It does not prove every household owned a horse, that mounted warriors ruled a state, or that the atlas polygon was patrolled. Burials record particular choices, not universal access.

Later museum collections preserve vessels, casks, farm tools, spinning equipment, bast-work tools, a bathhouse, and a granary from early twentieth-century village life. They make continuity questions visible while remaining eleven centuries too late to illustrate an 850 CE room without explicit qualification.

sections.title: Families, community, dress, and social difference

items.text: Paired graves and cemetery groupings may record relationships, but bones and proximity alone cannot establish a marriage rule, household size, clan system, inheritance pattern, or political office. Family certainly mattered; its exact organization in this window remains underdocumented. The card does not turn two nearby burials into a complete family tree.

Later studies describe homes as economic and ritual spaces shared by family groups, with work divided by age and gender. Because that evidence is retrospective and largely modern, it cannot supply ninth-century job assignments. It instead demonstrates why Erzya and Moksha domestic histories deserve dated, separate investigation.

A twentieth-century Erzya bride's costume and a nineteenth-century Moksha headdress have precise collection identities, places, dates, and materials. They show distinct later clothing traditions. Neither can be copied onto an eighth-century burial reconstruction, even when metal ornaments or textile traces look temptingly familiar.

The Volga and Ural region was multiethnic, and museum collections document exchange and cultural relationships among Mordovian, Russian, Tatar, and other communities. Medieval people also met neighbors, but shared objects do not erase difference. Interaction can produce borrowing, bilingualism, mixed households, or new styles without one uniform identity.

Modern family research follows changes in identity, gender, language, and generations through the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. That evidence belongs in continuity, not as a medieval template. It reminds readers that families transmit, revise, combine, or lose practices over time rather than carrying a sealed cultural package.

Children learned somehow because every skilled sequence had to be transmitted: preparing food, handling animals, making containers, dressing, navigating, crafting, and participating in ceremonies. Exact-period sources do not identify schools, lesson hours, teachers, writing tablets, or age grades. Learning is secure; its institutional form is not.

Separate Erzya and Moksha dialects and standards preserve considerable internal variation. Modern linguistic maps describe interspersed settlements, not two perfectly solid blocks. This warns against assigning a medieval child's language from one polygon, one ornament, or today's administrative boundary, even when later language geography seems convenient.

The Mormula corpus contains separately identified Erzya and Moksha folklore, literary prose, journalism, and translated material collected or published from the late nineteenth century onward. It supports study of storytelling and language transmission in documented eras, but no corpus text is presented as a ninth-century child's voice.

Twentieth-century Erzya-language teaching used schoolbooks, teachers, and a children's magazine in some settings. This is valuable continuity evidence with a date, not proof of a medieval school system. The card separates a modern classroom from earlier learning by watching, listening, practicing, remembering, and helping.

A 1928 Erzya song collection in the Russian National Electronic Library is tangible written heritage. Its catalogue date is secure, which makes it more useful than an undated claim of ancient literacy. Children could inherit songs much earlier orally, but this particular printed object belongs firmly to the twentieth century.

Burials show that communities cared for the dead, but the reviewed exact-period studies do not provide a population-wide account of disease, injury, nutrition, disability, childbirth, or lifespan. Grave objects cannot diagnose treatment. Silence about illness is an evidence gap, not proof that ninth-century people were unusually healthy.

A government humanities institute's 2011 ethnography records plant, animal, mineral, surgical, and spoken healing practices from much later fieldwork and historical sources. It demonstrates rich medical knowledge among documented communities. The card does not carry a remedy backward eleven centuries unless an exact archaeological or textual context supports it.

Field ethnography relies on observation, interviews, conversations, description, and classification. Those methods preserve living knowledge and memories, but memory has dates and contexts. A twentieth-century healer's practice may reflect continuity, innovation, neighboring influence, or individual experience; it cannot by itself prescribe what someone used in 850.

Food, shelter, fire, clothing, water, cooperation, and stored supplies affected health, while smoke, cold, injury, infection, and hunger created risks. These links are reasonable human inferences. Without direct skeletal, botanical, residue, or textual evidence, the card does not name a diagnosis, dosage, healer, or cure.

Ornaments, knives, and tools may have had practical, social, or ritual meanings. None becomes a medical instrument because it looks sharp or special. Secure medical interpretation needs context, use wear, residue, pathology, or a dated account. Otherwise an elegant object remains an elegant question, not a surprise surgery kit.

Cemeteries near the Middle Tsna demonstrate a river landscape, but burial location does not identify drinking-water sources, wells, buckets, filters, or household storage. Rivers could support travel, fishing, washing, and water collection while also flooding or carrying contamination. Exact routines for 800 to 900 remain unknown.

Later village museums preserve bathhouses, casks, and domestic vessels, evidence for washing and storage in a precisely later setting. They do not prove identical medieval plumbing. Wooden containers, floors, fences, and small structures also decay readily, making absence from excavation a preservation problem as well as a historical question.

Food scraps, ash, broken vessels, animal waste, craft debris, and worn objects had to be handled. Archaeology can sometimes locate deposits, yet the reviewed exact-period publications emphasize graves rather than settlement waste. No universal sweeping rule, rubbish service, or cleanliness standard can be reconstructed from that record.

No reviewed source securely identifies an 800 to 900 Erzya, Moksha, or Mordvinian toilet, latrine, sewer, drain, or fecal-waste routine. Organic facilities may vanish and settlements remain unevenly studied. This absence does not mean people lacked privacy; it means historians should not install imaginary medieval bathrooms.

Hearths, lamps, smithing, cooking, and heating produced useful warmth and light alongside smoke, sparks, and burns. Later craft evidence shows fire-dependent work, but exact ventilation is unrecorded. A safe card can discuss risks and maintenance without declaring that every home was smoky, spotless, or built to one plan.

Clothing traces and ornaments show fibre work, fastening, metalworking, dress, and careful assembly. Their preservation in graves is selective. Decorative choices may express age, occasion, community, relationship, or status, but a single pendant cannot translate identity. Craft skill is the secure achievement; one fixed social meaning is not.

Belt fittings crossed cultural and political zones, and researchers reject a simple equation between an elaborate belt and elite rank. Belts could hold equipment, display affiliation, or mark circumstances of burial. Comparison builds networks of possibility while leaving room for repair, reuse, gifts, copying, and personal choice.

Studies place Volga Bulgar-style belt sets in ancient-Mordvin cemeteries mainly in the tenth and eleventh centuries. That later dating matters. It demonstrates contact after the atlas window and prevents a ninth-century card from claiming every Bulgar-looking fitting as contemporary proof of tribute, alliance, conquest, or ethnicity.

Later Teryukhan archaeology documents farming, animals, hunting, fishing, beekeeping, metallurgy, pottery, spinning, weaving, and work in wood, bone, and leather. These varied accomplishments belong to a named later community and comparison horizon. They illuminate possibilities without becoming a checklist for all earlier Erzya and Moksha ancestors.

The strongest achievement is cumulative knowledge: adapting to river and forest environments, sustaining communities, making durable objects, exchanging ideas, and maintaining distinct languages through major political change. Archaeology rarely names an inventor. The card credits communities rather than manufacturing a heroic first potter, rider, healer, or grammarian.

sections.title: Texts, writing, and a securely dated sample

items.text: No locally authored Erzya or Moksha sentence survives from 800 to 900. Later chronicles use an outside collective label and were compiled centuries afterward. They help trace naming history, but they cannot reproduce a ninth-century conversation or prove that everyone inside the atlas polygon spoke one ancestral variety.

Modern literary Moksha, from the children's magazine Red Little Star 2/1994: “Монь ули алашазе.” Transcription: “monʲ ulʲ-i ɑlɑʃɑ-zʲæ.” Translation: “I have a horse.” Arja Hamari and Rigina Ajanki reproduce and gloss it as example 101, page 425, in their 2022 Oxford Guide chapter.

The sample belongs to modern standard Moksha and illustrates a possessive construction. It is not a quotation from a medieval rider, grave, or manuscript. Erzya has its own written standard and grammar. One short Moksha sentence cannot stand for Erzya, every dialect, or an undifferentiated “Mordvin language.”

Separate literary standards took shape much later, particularly in the twentieth century, although missionary-era writing reaches farther back. The University of Turku's diachronic corpus organizes dated Erzya and Moksha texts. A documented publication history is safer than inventing an ancient alphabet from ornaments or pottery marks.

Modern corpora combine newspapers, journals, fiction, folklore, and scholarly annotation while preserving language labels and provenance. They support language teaching and research today. Their abundance cannot fill the medieval documentary gap, yet it powerfully shows that the atlas endpoint did not end Erzya or Moksha expression.

The Russian Primary Chronicle lists Mordva among peoples with their own language, but the work was compiled in the twelfth century and survives in later manuscripts. Its outside label is important textual evidence after this card's interval. It is not a neutral ninth-century self-description or map of ethnic borders.

Later archaeological sites show exchange with Volga Bulgaria, Rus principalities, steppe networks, and neighboring forest peoples. Contacts could involve trade, conflict, movement, tribute, intermarriage, or craft transmission at different times. No single relationship explains every community, and later political histories cannot be poured backward into 800.

Russian and Soviet administration later grouped communities under Mordvinian and Mordovian categories, while people maintained, combined, or contested Erzya, Moksha, local, religious, and civic identities. The inherited 1928 sentence belongs here, inside modern history, rather than as the definition of a medieval civilization.

Collections in Estonia and elsewhere preserve objects and histories created through migration and collecting. Diaspora does not make identity less real or more uniform. It shows that Erzya and Moksha lives extend far beyond one republic, while museum labels themselves have histories that researchers should examine.

At 900 the polygon disappears, not the people. Archaeological classifications, political authorities, languages, settlements, and self-identifications changed on different schedules. Erzya and Moksha communities continue today. The responsible ending is transformation and continuity, with no invented conquest, extinction, merger, successor state, or moment of collective renaming.

ending.text: At 900 CE the exact mordvinians feature disappears from the atlas. That is a software seam, not evidence that a state fell or a people vanished. Broadly dated cemeteries continue beyond it; later chronicles use an external collective name; contacts with Volga Bulgaria, Rus, and neighboring forest communities develop on their own schedules; and the related Erzya and Moksha languages acquire separate documented standards much later. Modern administration often grouped distinct communities under Mordvinian or Mordovian labels, while self-identifications remained more varied. The card therefore has no named conqueror, predecessor, or successor. Its ending records transformation, uneven evidence, and continuing Erzya and Moksha peoples rather than extinction or a single political handover.
